title: Men and women for others
hookLine: Arrupe's phrase for what Jesuit education should form
last: HE TURNED THE HOUSE INTO A HOSPITAL.

cards: A room full of former students of Jesuit schools, gathered in Spain. Doctors, lawyers, business owners: comfortable people, proud of their schooling.
At the podium stands the same Pedro Arrupe, now the head of the whole Jesuit order. They might expect a warm speech about the old days.
Instead he asks a hard question: have Jesuit schools taught you to care about justice, or only to succeed? Then he offers a short phrase for what those schools are supposed to produce.
Tradition says some in the room did not like it. The phrase stayed anyway.

teach.b: Men and women for others. In Arrupe's own Spanish the talk was called hombres para los demás, men for others.
The aim of Jesuit education, he said, should be to form people who live not for themselves but for God and for others, especially the poor.
And he said something harder: that the schools had sometimes failed at it, and that he was asking forgiveness for that.
In time, as Jesuit schools welcomed girls and women, the phrase grew into men and women for others, the form you'll hear now. What makes it more than a slogan? Three things.

teach.h: WHO YOU BECOME, NOT ONLY WHAT YOU DO.
teach.b: It's about who you become, not only what you do. Volunteering on a Saturday is good; Arrupe was asking about the shape of a whole life.
It includes justice, not just charity: he wanted people to ask why someone is hungry, not only to hand them bread. And it's rooted in Jesus himself.
In Mark's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says the Son of man "is not come to be ministered unto: but to minister." Served, or serving: the phrase picks a side. Now the honest part.
For others can curdle into self-importance, the helper who needs to be needed.

teach.h: WHO WAS THE DAY REALLY FOR?
teach.b: The Ignatian answer is the examen: look back each night and ask who the day was really for.

teach.h: NOT TO BE MINISTERED UNTO, BUT TO MINISTER.
teach.b: For others might be as plain as letting someone go ahead in line, or as big as rethinking what your job is for.

how: Jesuit schools often describe their aim as forming men and women for others, and pair student service with reflection on it.

games.q: you're Arrupe, speaking to proud, successful former students. do you praise their success, or ask a hard question?
o: ask whether the schools taught them to live for others and for justice.
talk only about the history of the order.
games.why: he asked the hard question, and even asked forgiveness for where the schools had failed. tradition says some listeners were unhappy; the phrase lasted.

practice: Look ahead at the next day for one thing you could do for someone who didn't ask and won't pay you back, and make it concrete: a name, a task, a time.
Then ask the second question, the justice one: is there anything behind their need you could learn about, or speak up about? If you pray, offer the plan to God and ask for a clear heart in doing it.

wordCard.voice: Men and women for others. Pedro Arrupe's phrase for what Jesuit education should form: people who live for God and others, with justice, not only charity. Today's word.

orig.note: Spanish: men for others, the title of Arrupe's talk.

carryVoice: Your line: for others. Not to be served, but to serve, with justice as well as charity. Rest well.
